title: Spontaneous Emission
short_intro: Spontaneous emission is the quantum mechanical process by which an excited atomic system drops to a lower energy state by emitting a photon without external stimulation. The emitted photons are characterized by random phases, polarization, and directions of propagation.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definition, distinction between spontaneous and stimulated emission, role in ordinary light sources, and connection to energy levels.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Einstein A and B coefficient derivations, transition probabilities, lifetime of excited states, and spectral line broadening mechanisms.

prerequisites: Bohr's atomic model and energy quantization
Basic quantum mechanics and probability transition rates

concept_notes.heading: Mechanism of Spontaneous Emission
bullets: An electron in an excited state of energy E&sub2; naturally decays to a lower energy state E&sub1; after a characteristic mean lifetime (τ).
The energy difference ΔE = E&sub2; - E&sub1; is released in the form of a single photon of frequency ν = ΔE / h.
The process occurs entirely independently of any external radiation field, driven by zero-point fluctuations of the electromagnetic vacuum.

concept_notes.heading: Einstein's A Coefficient
bullets: The transition rate per unit time for an atom to spontaneously drop from state 2 to state 1 is denoted by the Einstein A coefficient, A&sub2;&sub1;.
The number of atoms decaying per second per unit volume is given by dN&sub2;/dt = -A&sub2;&sub1;N&sub2;.
The lifetime of the excited state is inversely proportional to the spontaneous emission rate, such that τ = 1 / A&sub2;&sub1;.

concept_notes.heading: Coherence and Directionality Characteristics
bullets: Photons emitted via spontaneous emission are mutually incoherent because each atom emits independently with a random phase.
The radiation propagates in random directions, leading to high spatial divergence characteristic of ordinary thermal and discharge sources.
The spectral output possesses a natural linewidth due to the finite lifetime of the excited state governed by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

concept_notes.heading: Comparison with Stimulated Emission
bullets: Unlike spontaneous emission, stimulated emission requires an incident photon of matching energy to trigger the downward transition.
Stimulated emission produces coherent photons identical in phase, frequency, polarization, and direction to the triggering photon, forming the basis of laser action.
At optical frequencies, spontaneous emission dominates over stimulated emission in thermal equilibrium due to the low population of high-energy states.

derivations.title: Relation Between Einstein A and B Coefficients
derivations.conditions: System in thermal equilibrium with a radiation field at absolute temperature T.
steps: Write the upward absorption rate as R&sub1;&sub2; = N&sub1;ρ(ν)B&sub1;&sub2; and downward emission rate as R&sub2;&sub1; = N&sub2;[A&sub2;&sub1; + ρ(ν)B&sub2;&sub1;], where ρ(ν) is the energy density of radiation.
Equate upward and downward rates in thermal equilibrium: N&sub1;ρ(ν)B&sub1;&sub2; = N&sub2;A&sub2;&sub1; + N&sub2;ρ(ν)B&sub2;&sub1;.
Rearrange to solve for energy density: ρ(ν) = A&sub2;&sub1; / [B&sub2;&sub1; ((N&sub1;/N&sub2;) - (B&sub1;&sub2;/B&sub2;&sub1;))].
Substitute the Boltzmann population ratio N&sub1;/N&sub2; = (g&sub2;/g&sub1;)exp(hν/kT) and match with Planck's radiation law ρ(ν) = (8πhν³/c³) / [exp(hν/kT) - 1].
Equating terms yields the relation between coefficients: A&sub2;&sub1; / B&sub2;&sub1; = 8πhν³/c³ and g&sub1;B&sub1;&sub2; = g&sub2;B&sub2;&sub1;.

derivations.title: Exponential Decay of Excited State Population
derivations.conditions: Absence of pumping and stimulated processes; pure spontaneous decay.
steps: Set up the rate equation for the population N&sub2; of the excited state: dN_2 / dt = -A_21 N_2.
Separate variables to integrate: int (1 / N_2) dN_2 = -A_21 int dt.
Perform integration to obtain ln(N_2) = -A_21 t + C.
Apply initial condition N_2(0) = N_0 to find C = ln(N_0).
Exponentiate both sides to get the final decay law N_2(t) = N_0 e^{-A_21 t}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Exponential Decay of Excited State Population
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of population N_2(t) on the y-axis versus time t on the x-axis, showing a downward concave exponential curve intersecting the y-axis at N_0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that the number of excited atoms decreases exponentially over time, with the time required for population to drop to 1/e of its initial value defined as the lifetime τ.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in MCQs to identify decay curves and calculate half-life or mean lifetime from graphical data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Energy Level Transition Diagram for Spontaneous Emission
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two horizontal lines representing energy levels E_1 and E_2 (with E_2 above E_1), connected by a wavy downward vertical arrow labeled with photon emission energy hν.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Depicts the downward transition of an electron from a higher unstable state to a lower stable state accompanied by the emission of a single photon.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used in conceptual questions distinguishing spontaneous emission, absorption, and stimulated emission.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Spectral Line Profile (Natural Broadening)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A symmetrical bell-shaped intensity (I) versus frequency (ν) curve, with full width at half maximum (FWHM) labeled as Δν.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that spontaneous emission is not perfectly monochromatic; due to the finite lifetime of the state, frequencies span a narrow Lorentzian distribution.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT level problems concerning line broadening mechanisms and uncertainty relations.

solved_numericals.question: An excited state of an atom has a mean lifetime of 10 ns. Calculate the Einstein A coefficient for this transition.
solution_steps: Identify the given lifetime: \tau = 10 \text{ ns} = 10 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s}.
Use the relation between lifetime and Einstein A coefficient: A_{21} = \frac{1}{\tau}.

solved_numericals.question: For a atomic transition at wavelength lambda = 6000 \text{ AA}, the Einstein A coefficient is 2 \times 10^7 \text{ s}^{-1}. Find the value of the Einstein B coefficient B_{21}.
solution_steps: Convert wavelength to meters: lambda = 6000 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m} = 6 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}.
Use the relation A_{21} / B_{21} = \frac{8pi h \nu^3}{c^3}.
Rearrange for B_{21}: B_{21} = \frac{A_{21} c^3}{8pi h \nu^3}.
Substitute values (h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}, c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}, A_{21} = 2 \times 10^7): B_{21} approx 2.44 \times 10^{19} \text{ m}^3 \text{ J}^{-1} \text{ s}^{-2}.

solved_numericals.question: If the initial population of an excited energy level is 5 \times 10^{18} \text{ atoms/cm}^3 and the spontaneous decay rate constant is 5 \times 10^7 \text{ s}^{-1}, find the population remaining after 20 \text{ ns}.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: N_0 = 5 \times 10^{18}, A_{21} = 5 \times 10^7 \text{ s}^{-1}, t = 20 \text{ ns} = 20 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s} = 2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ s}.
Use the decay formula: N_2(t) = N_0 e^{-A_{21} t}.
Compute population: N_2 = (5 \times 10^{18}) e^{-1} approx 5 \times 10^{18} \times 0.3678 = 1.839 \times 10^{18} \text{ atoms/cm}^3.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes two-level atomic systems interacting with isotropic blackbody radiation fields in thermodynamic equilibrium for Einstein coefficient derivations.
Neglects multi-photon emission processes and non-radiative decay mechanisms such as collisional quenching or Auger transitions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Spontaneous emission produces coherent light just like stimulated emission in lasers.
common_misconceptions.correct: Spontaneous emission produces incoherent light with random phases and directions.
common_misconceptions.why: Each atom decays independently without external phase referencing, unlike stimulated emission where the incoming photon forces phase coherence.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Spontaneous emission requires an external triggering photon.
common_misconceptions.correct: Spontaneous emission occurs entirely on its own without any external photon stimulus.
common_misconceptions.why: It is triggered by vacuum electromagnetic field fluctuations rather than incident radiation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Einstein A coefficient depends on temperature.
common_misconceptions.correct: Einstein A coefficient is an intrinsic atomic property independent of temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: A_21 depends only on atomic wavefunctions and transition dipole moments, whereas radiation density depends on temperature.

quick_revision: Spontaneous emission is the unprovoked downward transition of an electron emitting an incoherent photon: A_21 = 1 / \tau.
Excited State Population Decay: N_2(t) = N_0 e^{-t/\tau}
